# Azure Resource Manager Container Instance client library for Java

Azure Resource Manager Container Instance client library for Java

For documentation on how to use this package, please see [Azure Management Libraries for Java](https://aka.ms/azsdk/java/mgmt).

## Getting started

### Prerequisites

- [Java Development Kit (JDK)][jdk] with version 8 or above
- [Azure Subscription][azure_subscription]

### Adding the package to your product

[//]: # ({x-version-update-start;com.azure.resourcemanager:azure-resourcemanager-containerinstance;current})
```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.azure.resourcemanager</groupId>
    <artifactId>azure-resourcemanager-containerinstance</artifactId>
    <version>2.54.0-beta.1</version>
</dependency>
```
[//]: # ({x-version-update-end})

### Include the recommended packages

Azure Management Libraries require a `TokenCredential` implementation for authentication and an `HttpClient` implementation for HTTP client.

[Azure Identity][azure_identity] package and [Azure Core Netty HTTP][azure_core_http_netty] package provide the default implementation.

### Authentication

Microsoft Entra ID token authentication relies on the [credential class][azure_identity_credentials] from [Azure Identity][azure_identity] package.

Azure subscription ID can be configured via `AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID` environment variable.
Azure tenant ID can be configured via `AZURE_TENANT_ID` environment variable.

Assuming the use of the `DefaultAzureCredential` credential class, the client can be authenticated using the following code:

```java readme-sample-authenticate
AzureProfile profile = new AzureProfile(AzureCloud.AZURE_PUBLIC_CLOUD);
TokenCredential credential = new DefaultAzureCredentialBuilder()
    .authorityHost(profile.getEnvironment().getActiveDirectoryEndpoint())
    .build();
ContainerInstanceManager manager = ContainerInstanceManager
    .authenticate(credential, profile);
```

The sample code assumes global Azure. Please change `AzureEnvironment.AZURE` variable if otherwise.

See [Authentication][authenticate] for more options.

## Key concepts

decisions.reason: The two authenticate overloads and configurable delegate are visible, but this whole class has no generated/unannotated contrast or customization-script provenance. Conventional manager factory and null-check code alone cannot establish handwritten ownership.

The concrete manager assembles the lower-level client and three other service managers using a shared pipeline/profile, a substantive cross-service facade over fluent generated operations rather than an emitted client method. The proposal describes that construction without asserting an unseen dependency contract; its composition pattern is service-independent and general generation remains unclear.
The lazy cached accessor is present, but neither a generated marker comparison nor a customization operation establishes that this standard collection accessor was handwritten.

The resource implementation explicitly switches update versus create request payloads and stages external identity and share dependencies; this is concrete high-level orchestration, not a generated LRO or simple forwarding method. The proposed conditional-dispatch pattern is reusable; its generator feasibility is appropriately unclear.

The cited methods construct a separate network/subnet resource, bind its identifier, and invoke the stored creatable before the group operation. Cross-service fluent composition is substantive customization; the proposal correctly leaves framework ordering and generator feasibility unresolved.

The implementation stages a new or existing-group storage account as a resource dependency and records pending volume/share names. This distinct dependent-resource recipe is visible in the handwritten-style facade, and the proposed generic pattern does not assume unobserved dependency execution.

The supplied body gets a storage key, constructs a separate file-share SDK client using the manager's HTTP client, creates shares, and projects volume parameters. This cross-SDK composition is substantive and distinct from merely staging a storage account; the proposed caveat about not sharing the entire pipeline is correct.

The custom preparation callback blocks dependency tasks, prepares identities and file shares, and attaches volumes before supplying a typed resource adapter to AcceptedImpl. Those supplied callbacks are additional resource behavior, not a claim that the unseen AcceptedImpl poller itself is handwritten; the proposal expressly limits that claim.

The resource reconstructs named child maps and registry-server projections from its inner model at construction, after creation, and after refresh. That lifecycle-aware derived state is a substantive facade customization rather than generated model serialization; the proposal does not claim deep copies or unshown accessor behavior.

The implementation sets absent protocols to TCP and derives port arrays in the resource facade. The proposal accurately records that the second fill loop mistakenly writes TCP values into externalTcpPorts rather than populating externalUdpPorts, without claiming a proven public symptom or intended correction; generator feasibility remains unclear.
The fixed Linux/Windows setters are present, but the absence of a generation marker throughout the file does not establish that these conventional fluent methods were hand-added rather than emitted.

The resource-specific MSI handler implements nontrivial type combination and initialization of an inner identity model, beyond an authentication policy or generated property setter. The cited invalid-value branch and lack of an explicit null guard are faithfully distinguished; the proposed service-independent identity-composition pattern is plausible.

The helper adds creatable identities to the task graph, resolves their keys to identity IDs, and writes a user-assigned-identity model map. This cross-resource dependency binding is substantive facade behavior; the proposal confines execution claims to the visible methods and leaves generator feasibility unclear.

The resource explicitly exposes role/scope overloads routed through an authorization-manager-backed helper with its task group and ID provider. The cited bodies support this handwritten-style cross-service bridge, but not the inherited role-assignment implementation or any bearer-token customization; the proposal says so.

The registry-credential overloads and model mutation are visible, but no per-member generated contrast or script establishes their provenance. The broad model-wire-adapter label also obscures the specific alternative-credential construction shape, so acceptance as written is unwarranted.
The method appends a named empty-directory model with an empty-object marker, but the supplied source cannot distinguish a generated fluent builder from a handwritten model-construction override.
